posts.title: Indianapolis Chamber Orchestra feels the pulse of America's 250th anniversary
posts.description: Melissa White melted hearts with the Barber concerto. With the current head of state focused mainly on how important he is, it has not been surprising to find that lots of the celebration around the United States' semiquincentennial has come from cultural organizations, not the government. The Indianapolis Chamber Orchestra registered its tribute Saturday night under the straightforward title "Pulse." It was an all-American program at the Schrott Center , divided between two living composers and two from anyone's American hall of fame. Melissa White, first-prize winner in the Sphinx Competition and a founding member of the Harlem Quartet, provided the glamour on the performing side of the concert. Tucker Fuller was on hand to introduce his "Limerence," one of two commissioned works on the ICO's 2026-27 season, in its world premiere. posts.title: UIndy guest recital: Clarifying Ravel even more than what he set down on the page
posts.description: Hyeseon Jin has a doctorate from IU I knew as soon as I saw the program of a guest recitalist at the University of Indianapolis that I would want to be there. In fact I had sort of forgot everything else Hyeseon Jin was scheduled to play until I was seated in the Ruth Lilly Performance Hall Friday evening. What put the performance in the "must-hear" category for me was Maurice Ravel's "La Valse," which can dependably wow an orchestra audience but is much less often encountered as a solo piano piece. Grove's Dictionary even says the piano version is for two pianos. Its difficulty under a mere two hands is one thing, but of course it's a magnificent concept and a tapestry honoring the Viennese waltz with unparalleled fervor. You'll come across symphony program notes that make a lot of the extramusical meaning of the work as a foreshadowing the late 19th- century world about to be blown to smithereens by World War I. posts.title: Ensemble Music Society debut: Formosa Quartet puts the fun foremost
posts.description: There was no question of Brahms being an afterthought for the Cover of the group's McKay recording Formosa Quartet Wednesday night after it offered a lively "collection of our curiosities" just before intermission of its Ensemble Music Society appearance at the Glick Indiana History Center. The phrase came from violinist David Bernat to describe the Formosa Quartet "set" after the ensemble played its opening piece, George Frederick McKay's "American Sketches." That work gave sufficient evidence of the group's right to be making its EMS debut. McKay's language across the three movements of his String Quartet No. 1 is thick-textured but with no cluttering in the flow of ideas. Syncopation and a "hoedown" atmosphere (Copland offers a ready comparison in "Rodeo") were attractively mastered in the finale.
